column1: merge|How does merging differ from rebasing a Git branch?|A merge combines histories and can preserve a merge commit; a rebase replays commits onto a new base and usually creates new commit IDs. Choose according to collaboration policy, and do not rewrite shared history casually. Resolve and test semantic conflicts in either approach.|history;replay~commit;IDs~rewrite;shared|Rebase preserves every original commit ID.|A teammate based work on your published feature branch. Should you rebase it silently?|Coordinate first because rewritten commit IDs can disrupt their history. Merge or agree on a rebase/update procedure; if force-pushing is allowed prefer force-with-lease and understand its protection limits.|git-rebase|replay

rebase-conflict|What should be done after resolving a rebase conflict?|Inspect the conflict in the replayed commit's new context, stage the intended resolution, and use git rebase --continue. Use --abort to return to the pre-rebase state where appropriate. Test the resulting history; textual conflict resolution does not prove correctness.|stage;--continue;--abort;test|Resolving conflict markers proves the rebased program is correct.|A rebase completed without conflicts but changed behavior. What investigation should follow?|Compare the rebased changes and relevant base commits, run focused tests, inspect semantic interactions, and use the reflog or saved branch to compare pre-rebase state.|git-rebase|continue

ci-isolation|How should a CI failure be isolated before changing application code?|Capture the exact failing command, commit, runtime/toolchain, environment, and dependency lock state. Reproduce a focused failure, compare a known-good run, and separate infrastructure or permission failures from deterministic regressions. Preserve useful sanitized logs and artifacts.|command;version~environment;known-good~reproduc;infrastructure~permission|Every red CI job proves application code is wrong.|A test passes locally but fails only in Linux CI. Give a concrete isolation plan.|Run the locked dependency versions and exact command under the CI OS/runtime, inspect case-sensitive paths, time zones, resources and secrets, and minimize to a reproducible test before patching.|github-workflow,sre-testing|runner

bisect|How does git bisect locate a regression and what does its test oracle require?|Mark a known good and bad revision, then test selected commits to narrow the range. git bisect run automates an oracle whose exit status distinguishes good, bad, and skipped revisions. The test must be reliable and commits must be testable or explicitly skipped.|good;bad;oracle~exit;skip|An unreliable flaky test is a sound bisect oracle.|A regression test cannot run on some intermediate commits. How should an automated bisect handle them?|Return git bisect run's skip status 125 for untestable revisions, good status 0 for passing revisions, and a bad status otherwise within documented rules. Record ambiguous ranges rather than fabricating a single culprit.|git-bisect|125

flaky-ci|How can flaky CI tests be distinguished from deterministic regressions?|Repeat the exact test with recorded seed, order, runtime, and resources; isolate shared state, timing, race, and external dependency effects. Quarantine only with ownership and a repair plan. Retries can collect evidence but should not hide the failure rate.|seed~repeat;shared~race;timing~order;quarantine~repair|Adding unlimited retries fixes the underlying flaky test.|A test fails one in twenty CI runs but a retry passes. What evidence should be collected before merging a fix?|Persist random seed, ordering, timestamps or traces, and worker topology; reproduce with deterministic scheduling or fake clocks where possible and measure failure rate before and after.|sre-testing,node-test|flaky

needs|What does GitHub Actions needs establish, and how do failed dependencies affect downstream jobs?|needs defines a job dependency graph and exposes dependency results and outputs. By default a dependent job requires successful dependencies; failure or skipping can skip downstream work unless an appropriate explicit condition applies. It is not a sharing mechanism for arbitrary filesystem state.|dependency;success~skip;result~output;artifact~filesystem|Every job with needs runs even if its dependencies fail.|A report job needs a failing test job and never starts. How can reporting be arranged safely?|Use an intentional status condition such as always() where suitable, inspect needs.test.result, and make report inputs robust to missing artifacts. Avoid an unconditional deployment on failed tests.|github-workflow|needs

always-cancel|Does if: always() make a GitHub Actions job immune to cancellation or timeout?|always() is a status-check condition that can evaluate true even after cancellation; it is not immunity from all forced termination, timeouts, or missing inputs. For work that should stop on cancellation consider !cancelled() and explicit dependency-result checks. Bound cleanup work.|cancel;timeout~termination;!cancelled~condition;bounded~cleanup|always() guarantees a job can never be cancelled or timed out.|A cleanup job with always() hangs while fetching unavailable dependencies during cancellation. Redesign it.|Avoid unbounded dependency fetching in unconditional cleanup. Use local best-effort cleanup with a timeout and an appropriate cancelled/result condition; ensure missing prior outputs do not deadlock it.|github-workflow|always()

permissions|How should GITHUB_TOKEN permissions be configured?|Grant the minimum permissions needed at workflow or job level. Explicit permission configuration can set unspecified permissions to none according to workflow rules. Review token availability, repository policy, and action behavior rather than assuming write access.|least~minimum;job~workflow;none;token|Every workflow should receive write-all by default.|A test-only workflow requests contents: write and packages: write. What should be changed?|Reduce to the required read or no permissions and separate release operations into controlled jobs. Pin trusted dependencies and avoid handing privileged tokens to untrusted code.|github-workflow,github-security|permissions

forks|What restrictions commonly apply to GitHub Actions workflows from fork pull requests?|Secrets normally are not passed to ordinary fork pull-request workflows and GITHUB_TOKEN is read-only unless repository/enterprise policy explicitly changes behavior. Approval settings may apply. Treat fork code as untrusted and do not bypass these boundaries by exposing credentials.|secret;read-only~read only;fork;policy|Fork pull requests always receive repository secrets.|A fork test fails because a deployment secret is absent. How should the pipeline be redesigned?|Keep untrusted PR tests secret-free and run deployment only after a trusted review boundary. Use mocks or public fixtures for tests rather than printing or forwarding secrets to the fork.|github-security|fork

pr-target|Why is pull_request_target dangerous when combined with checkout of untrusted PR code?|pull_request_target runs in a privileged base-repository context depending on configuration. Checking out and executing attacker-controlled PR code there can expose secrets or writable tokens. Separate metadata-only trusted automation from untrusted code execution.|base~privileg;untrusted;secret~token;separate|pull_request_target makes arbitrary PR code safe to run with secrets.|An action uses pull_request_target, checks out the PR head, then runs its npm install scripts. Review the trust boundary.|Untrusted install scripts can execute in a privileged context. Do not run the PR head with those credentials; use an unprivileged pull_request test path and narrowly scoped trusted follow-up.|github-security|pull_request_target

subprocess|How should a Node application execute a command with untrusted arguments safely?|Use spawn or execFile with a fixed executable and an argument array, avoiding shell interpolation. Validate allowed options and working directories, limit resources, and protect secrets. Argument arrays prevent shell metacharacter interpretation but do not prevent an invoked program's option injection.|argument~array;fixed~executable;shell;validat~option|Passing user text through a shell is safe whenever it is wrapped in quotes.|A filename beginning with -- is passed to a CLI via execFile. Is avoiding the shell sufficient?|No. The CLI may interpret it as an option. Validate the interface and use an end-of-options marker where supported; keep the executable fixed and handle the returned status.|node-child,github-security|shell

bash-default|What does ${name:-fallback} do in Bash when name is unset or empty?|It expands to fallback when the parameter is unset or null, without assigning fallback to name. The colon makes the empty-string case count as missing; ${name-fallback} checks only whether it is unset. Quote expansions when appropriate.|unset;empty~null;without assign~not assign~does not assign;colon|The :- expansion always assigns the fallback to the variable.|name is empty. After echo "${name:-guest}", what value does name have?|The command prints guest but name remains empty. Use the assignment form only when mutation is intended.|bash|:-

bash-assign|How does ${name:=fallback} differ from ${name:-fallback} in Bash?|The := form assigns the fallback when name is unset or null and expands that value; :- only substitutes during expansion. Assignment is not allowed for every kind of shell parameter, such as positional or special parameters. Quoting and command-substitution side effects still matter.|assign;unset;empty~null;substitut|The := and :- expansions have identical assignment behavior.|A script wants to remember the default output directory for later commands. Which expansion is appropriate?|Use a deliberate assignment such as : "${output_dir:=build}" for a normal variable, then quote "$output_dir". A :- expansion alone would not persist the default.|bash|:=

pipe-status|What exit status does a Bash pipeline return and how does pipefail change it?|Normally the pipeline status is that of its last command. With pipefail it is the rightmost nonzero status, or zero if all succeed. PIPESTATUS can expose individual statuses but must be captured before another command replaces it.|last;rightmost~nonzero;pipefail;PIPESTATUS|A pipeline always reports the first command's failure by default.|A failing producer pipes into a successful consumer and CI reports success. How should failure be detected?|Enable pipefail where suitable or capture PIPESTATUS immediately and handle each component. Do not assume set -e alone changes the pipeline's default status rule.|bash|pipefail

set-e|Why is set -e not a complete Bash error-handling strategy?|errexit has context-dependent exceptions, including tests and many conditional or pipeline positions, and command substitutions have additional rules. Explicitly check critical command statuses, use deliberate cleanup traps, and preserve the original exit status rather than blindly trusting set -e.|exception~conditional;status;trap~cleanup;explicit|set -e guarantees termination after every nonzero command in every context.|A cleanup trap runs a failing command and accidentally replaces the original build error. How should it be written?|Save the original status immediately, perform bounded best-effort cleanup, and exit with the saved status. Test the exact shell and conditional contexts used in CI.|bash|errexit
